title: Leaders & Luminaries: Special Operations to Business Operations: One UT Dallas Alumnus’s Journey from the Battlefield to the Boardroom
description:
Join us for the Leaders and Luminaries series featuring guest speaker John Goodson, EPPS Alumnus and Founder/CEO of Darkhive Inc.

Darkhive Inc., is a Texasbased defense tech firm that builds seamlessly integrated hardware and software solutions for the modern battlefield. John is both a U.S.military veteran and a seasoned defense tech executive. As a Special Operations veteran, John has been on the frontlines of conflict, having completed four tours of duty in Afghanistan as a combat technician supporting the West Coast Navy SEAL Teams. John received multiple awards and citations, including the Navy and Marine Corps Commendation Medal with Combat “V” designation for valor. As an industry leader, John understands firsthand the cost of mission failure and is driven to deliver adaptable, scalable, cutting-edge systems designed to achieve mission success for those who serve.


This event is open to all! Refreshments will be provided.

Date: Monday, April13, 2026 Time: 11:00am – 1:00pm Location: McDermott Suite (MC 4.404) 
Please RSVP here.

title: Collegiate Recovery Week's Dimension Days: Home
description:
Join the Center for Students in Recovery, the Basic Needs Resource Center, the Comet Cupboard, and Residential Life as we take part in recognizing Collegiate Recovery Week by exploring one of the four dimensions of recovery - home. SAMHSA (Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration) defines home in supporting life in recovery as a stable and safe place to live.

During this event students will have the chance to create and paint their own birdhouses! Snacks will be available while supplies last.

The event will take place on Monday, April 13th from 1:00pm – 3:00pm at the first floor of the Student Union (by the pool tables).
No registration required. For any questions, please contact recovery@utdallas.edu.

We hope to see you there!

title: Collegiate Recovery Week's Dimension Days: Purpose
description:
Join the Center for Students in Recovery, the University Career Center, and the Office of Student Volunteerism as we take part in recognizing Collegiate Recovery Week by exploring one of the four dimensions of recovery - purpose. SAMHSA (Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration) defines purpose as meaningful daily activities and the independence, income, and resources to participate in society.

During this event students will have the opportunity to participate in activities focused on purpose towards self and the community.

  • Students will get to partake in career exploration and designing different paths for their own future with the Career Center.
  • Students will also get to design Bye Bye Bags (lunch size paper sacks) and fill them with shelf-stable snacks. All of the Bye Bye Bags created will be donated to the Vogel Alcove - an organization that assists young children and families.

The event will take place on Wednesday, April 15th from 1:00pm – 3:00pm at the first floor of the Student Union (by the pool tables).
No registration required. For any questions, please contact recovery@utdallas.edu.

We hope to see you there!

title: Synthetic Bloom Panel
description:
Synthetic Bloom is a collaborative curatorial project between Professors Brynn Higgins-Stirrup and Diana Rojas to explore the current state of AI and its impact on society and the environment. Is AI a tool of truth—revealing human patterns and histories through its algorithms—or a tool of distortion—creating multi-layered realities?

Join us for a panel featuring academics and interdisciplinary creative practitioners. Panelists will share their work and insights on visual art, technology, AI, music, and experience, followed by a short Q&A session. This event is open to the public.

 

Panelists:

Dr. Marco B. Nardelli
Regents Professor,
University of North Texas

Kerry Maguire, MFA
Visiting Professor of Practice
Southern Methodist University

Dr. Tyson E. Lewis
Professor,
University of North Texas

Christopher Meerdo, MFA
Assistant Professor,
University of North Texas

Moderated by Professors Diana Rojas and Brynn Higgins-Stirrup.

Light refreshments will be served while supplies last.

title: OBCC Spring 2026 Gather & Grow Networking Mixer
description:
Join OBCC for an evening of meaningful connection and conversation at our Spring 2026 Gather & Grow Networking Mixer. This event brings together alumni, current students, and prospective professionals to build relationships, exchange ideas, and strengthen our leadership community.

Enjoy light refreshments, complimentary professional headshots, and an engaging keynote from OBCC instructor Neeru Sharma.

In her talk, Neeru explores how leadership is evolving in a world shaped by AI and rapid technological change. As automation and intelligent systems influence how we work and make decisions, leadership is less about having all the answers and more about cultivating the right mindset. She will discuss the growing importance of human-centered leadership and the real challenges leaders face today, including navigating uncertainty, leading through constant change, building trust in hybrid and technology-supported environments, and strengthening judgment where human insight still matters most. This session invites leaders to reflect on what it truly means to lead in an AI-driven world, starting from within.

We look forward to welcoming you for an evening of connection, insight, and community.

title: Cross-Layer Optimization of RF Architectures and Algorithms for Secure, Energy-Constrained Wireless Systems by Rabia Tugce Yazicigil, Boston Univserity
description:
Bio: 

Rabia Tugce Yazicigil is an Associate Professor in the Department of Electrical and Computer Engineering at Boston University and a Network Faculty member at Sabanci University. She was a Postdoctoral Associate at MIT and received her Ph.D. degree from Columbia University in 2016. Her research lies at the intersection of integrated circuits, biosensing, signal processing, hardware security, and wireless communications, with a focus on system-level innovations for future energy-constrained applications.

Dr. Yazicigil has received numerous honors, including the NSF CAREER Award (2024), the Boston University College of Engineering Early Career Excellence in Research Award (2024), the Catalyst Foundation Award (2021), the BU ENG Dean’s Catalyst Award (2021), and the Electrical Engineering Collaborative Research Award for her Ph.D. work (2016).

She currently serves as Chair of the Solid-State Circuits Society (SSCS) Women-in-Circuits Committee and was selected as a member of the 2015 MIT EECS Rising Stars cohort. She is an IEEE SSCS and CASS Distinguished Lecturer for the 2024–2026 term, was elected to the IEEE SSCS Administrative Committee as a Member-at-Large in 2024, and currently serves as Chair of the IEEE SSCS Distinguished Lecture Program. In 2024, she was also selected as a member of the National Academy of Engineering (NAE) U.S. Frontiers of Engineering cohort.

Dr. Yazicigil has served as an Associate Editor for IEEE Transactions on Circuits and Systems I and IEEE Transactions on Circuits and Systems for Artificial Intelligence, and she is a Technical Program Committee member of IEEE RFIC.

Abstract: 

This talk presents a holistic framework for enhancing physical-layer security and spectral efficiency in energy-constrained wireless systems. The approach integrates information- and task-centric algorithms with advanced RF architectures to enable secure and energy-efficient operation. Central to this work is a cross-layer design methodology that unifies RF hardware, signal processing, and embedded security. The ultimate goal is to establish an application-driven framework that enables scalable, reliable, and energy-efficient solutions for next-generation wireless systems.

Rabia Tugce Yazicigil is an Associate Professor in the Department of Electrical and Computer Engineering at Boston University and a Network Faculty member at Sabanci University. She was a Postdoctoral Associate at MIT and received her Ph.D. degree from Columbia University in 2016. Her research lies at the intersection of integrated circuits, biosensing, signal processing, hardware security, and wireless communications, with a focus on system-level innovations for future energy-constrained applications.

Dr. Yazicigil has received numerous honors, including the NSF CAREER Award (2024), the Boston University College of Engineering Early Career Excellence in Research Award (2024), the Catalyst Foundation Award (2021), the BU ENG Dean’s Catalyst Award (2021), and the Electrical Engineering Collaborative Research Award for her Ph.D. work (2016).

title: Call Me Dancer: Film Screening & Live Dance Performance
description:
Movement and Mentorship

Experience Call Me Dancer, a highly acclaimed, award-winning, and inspiring documentary about pursuing artistic dreams against the odds, paired with the debut of an original live dance performance created in collaboration with thinkIndia Foundation and the Indian Student Association at UT Dallas. Following the screening, filmmaker Leslie Shampaine, will be joined by members of thinkIndia and ISA for a reflective discussion about the film’s themes, the power of dance to unite community, and the ways we learn from one another and grow collectively.

This evening celebrates dance not only as performance, but as resilience, connection, and possibility. Together, the performance, film, and conversation invite audiences to consider what it means to take creative risks, embrace uncertainty, and to find belonging through movement.

Program schedule: 

6:00 p.m.                      Doors Open
6:30-7:00 p.m.             Live Dance Performance
7:00-8:30 p.m.             Film Screening
8:30-9:00 p.m.             Panel Discussion
9:00-9:45 p.m.             Reception with light refreshments

About the Film:

Manish is an athletic street dancer from India, whose working-class parents are depending on their only son for support. When he accidentally walks into a dance school and encounters Yehuda, a curmudgeonly 75-year-old ballet master, a passion ignites within him. Despite all odds, he is determined to make it professionally. Together, this unlikely duo embarks on a journey that transforms both of their lives.

1 hour and 24 minutes; TV-PG

About Leslie Shampaine:

Leslie Shampaine has been telling stories throughout her professional life. From the ballet stage where she performed across the world during a 13-year career, to the television screen where she has produced award-winning programs for PBS, Discovery Channel, A&E, CBS, and Al Jazeera​ Her work ranges from documentaries to cultural and educational series and includes 8 years as part of the production team for the Emmy award-winning Kennedy Center Honors.

In 2024, she was awarded a Fulbright Scholarship to India, where she led workshops and film screenings. Her work continues to build global connections, bridging cultures through storytelling, mentorship, and a deep commitment to the arts.

About thinkIndia Foundation:

thinkIndia is a fully volunteer driven organization. They connect with people in the community to create spectacular Broadway-style theatrical productions as well as art & culture exhibits and associated programming, and use the proceeds to care for those in need by supporting charitable causes and promoting the arts.

About Indian Student Association:

The Indian Students Association (ISA) is a non-profit socio-cultural association within the Student Organization's Forum at The University of Texas at Dallas, which is home to thousands of Indian students. ISA represents every one of them and strives to make each student feel at home. Even thousands of miles from India, ISA draws colorful Indian culture through its various programs throughout the calendar year. A key purpose of ISA is to provide ample opportunity for all students of Indian origin to interact, share, and educate about the culture and heritage of India amongst themselves as well as the UTD community at large.

Parking & Directions to the Edith O'Donnell Arts and Technology Building (ATC)

For best access to ATC, park in Parking Structure 1 (PS1)

📍 2500 Drive G, Richardson, TX 75080


Please park in Gold and/or Orange spaces only.

On-campus Driving Directions to PS1:

  • From Floyd Road, turn west onto Bryce Jordan Drive
  • Turn south onto Drive G
  • Enter Parking Structure 1 (PS1)

Walking Directions from PS1:

  • Exit PS1 and head west toward campus
  • Walk past the Davidson-Gundy Alumni Center (DGA)
  • The ATC building will be directly behind DGA

Download instructions and map here.
 

Advanced registration encouraged.

title: Learn How to BYOL (Bring Your Own Lunch): Grad Student Appreciation Week
description:
Register: https://calendly.com/utdoge/learn-how-to-byol 

Packing lunch can be healthier and less expensive, but it also requires supplies, time, and access to a place to store it. Bianca Schinzer, Assistant Director of Healthy Comets and Nutrition at the UTD Student Wellness Center, will provide practical advice on how to pack a lunch that survives the stresses of your day and what to pack so you'll want to eat it. Box lunches will be available AND attendees will each receive a reusable UTD lunch bag! Registration is required.

title: Hands-On Arduino & IoT Workshop
description:
Are you ready to bring your ideas to life and step into the future of technology? Join us for an action-packed, hands-on Intro to Arduino and IoT Workshop where you'll cross the bridge from pure software to physical reality! In this high-energy session, you will learn the fundamentals of building smart devices, writing code to control hardware, and connecting everyday objects to the internet. Whether you are a curious beginner or a tech enthusiast looking to expand your skills, you will work with actual microcontrollers to read live sensor data, control physical components, and unlock the endless possibilities of the Internet of Things...no prior hardware experience required!

✅ Beginner-friendly | ✅ Hands-on | ✅ Great for robotics/IoT beginners
💻 Students must bring their own laptop (required). |  🥤Snacks & Drinks
🎟️ Seats are limited—register early.

Register before 1:00pm on Friday, April 10:  forms.gle/oCcnmJzayGD4kHKA

  • Date:  Saturday, April 11th
  • Time:  10:00am - 1:00pm
  • Location:  ECSN 2.704

Food: Pizza

Open to All Majors and Minors !!!

Comets near and far are called to gather in celebration of 50 years of the Harry W. Bass Jr. School of Arts, Humanities, & Technology. 

Commemorate 50 years of being BOLD with a live performance by BASS student musicians, followed by remarks by Dean Roemer and a special retrospective video package five decades in the making!

Our very own BASS labs & studios will be presenting works in open house exhibitions, but first, make sure you get your POPCORN AND ICE CREAM!

Check back for more info to drop. In the meantime, BE BOLD, BE BASS.

title: Spring 2026 MSE Student Seminar Series
description:
The upcoming seminar will benefit all MSE students, however as a scholar with similar research interests, your participation in the Q&A session will help maximize your benefit from the talk, and ensure that professional academic etiquette is extended to the spearker, with an engaged student audience. MSE students meet monthly to witness a MSE PhD candidate present research interests, practice proposal presentations, and provide feedback to defend their dissertation. title: Spring Public Lecture featuring Wendy Rogers, PhD, University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign
description:
The Center for Vital Longevity is proud to present Dr. Wendy Rogers, University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign, as the 2026 Spring Public Lecture invited guest speaker.  Dr. Rogers will present TBA. 

More information coming soon.

This event is FREE and open to the public. Seating is limited, register early to save your seat. 

EVENT PROGRAM:

4:30 PM  Reception

5:00 PM  Lecture

6:15 PM  CVL Poster Exhibit

About the speaker: Wendy A. Rogers, PhD, is Khan Professor of Applied Health Sciences at the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign.  She is a Certified Human Factors Professional (BCPE #1539).  She is Director of the McKechnie Family LIFE Home; Program Director of CHART (Collaborations in Health, Aging, Research, & Technology); and Director of the Human Factors and Aging Laboratory.  Her research focuses on advanced technology design to support autonomy of older adults, with and without disabilities.  She explores the benefits of technologies including robots, smart-home technology, digital health, wearables, and telehealth for cognitive, physical, and emotional health.

 

The annual Spring Lecture is hosted in partnership with the Texas Instruments Alumni Association and made possible by the Jean & Bill Booziotis Distinguished Lecture funds.

title: From Gaze to Growth: A Developmental Framework for Social Communication & Language | BBS Distinguished Lecture
description:
Speaker: Dr. Pamela Rollins
Professor
School of Behavioral and Brain Sciences – Department of Speech, Language, and Hearing
The University of Texas at Dallas

Title: Migraine:  The Mysterious and Most Common Neurological Disorder

Abstract: Social communication emerges from early, coordinated interactions between children and caregivers. Grounded in Tomasello’s theory of shared intentionality, this talk investigates mutual gaze and social responsiveness as foundational building blocks for social communication and language in young autistic children. Over the past decade, a program of randomized controlled trials has evaluated a parent-mediated early autism intervention targeting these social processes. Findings show meaningful, transferable gains in social communication and expressive language across culturally and linguistically diverse families. Emerging AI-based measurement tools enable more precise, ecologically valid assessment of mutual gaze and will be described in relation to both research and clinical practice. Together, these efforts position early social interaction as a foundation for communication development and offer guidance for developmentally and culturally informed interventions.

Don't miss this chance to hear from a leading mind in the field — and walk away with fresh perspectives to fuel your own work.

This talk will be held in-person at the Polykarp Kusch Auditorium FN 2.102 and streamed live via MS Teams.

Join on MS Teams | See more BBS events

title: Mathematical Sciences Colloquium: The Finite Groups of Random Walks in the Quarter Plane and Periodic 4-bar Links; Vladimir Dragovic, University of Texas at Dallas
description: We present our solutions to two long standing open problems, the first one from probability theory, formulated by Malyshev in 1970 and the second one from a crossroad of geometry and dynamics, posed by Darboux in 1879. The Malyshev problem is of finding effective, explicit necessary and sufficient conditions in the closed form to characterize all random walks in the quarter plane with the group of the random walk of order 2n, for all n ≥ 2. The previously known results covered the cases n=2, 3, and 4. We describe all n-periodic Darboux transformations for 4-bar link problems for all n ≥ 2, thus completely solving the Darboux problem, that he solved for n = 2 in 1879 and Izmestiev for n=3 in 2023. This is based on a joint work with Milena Radnovic (arXiv: 2512:21976).

title: Mathematical Sciences Colloquium: Fox coloring, Alexander matrix, and Burau representation; Jozef H. Przytycki, Professor, George Washington Universityentation,
description: I describe a path from the Kauffman–Harary conjecture on Fox colorings to the Burau representation of links and the linearity of braid groups. As a case study, we analyze the family of braids (s_1s_2^{-1})^n, known as wheel or Turk’s Head braids; the case n=3 yields the Borromean rings. The faithfulness of the 4-string Burau representation remains an open problem.

title: OSIM Research Seminar Series - Dr. Aaron Hill

raw_payload.title: OSIM Research Seminar Series - Dr. Aaron Hill

custom_fields.excerpt:
Thematic Overview and Early-Stage Extensions for Feedback and Discussion

Abstract:  Reflecting on the diverse group of research interest and varying career stages, I offer a thematic overview of my research interests and early-stage extensions of recent methodological research which I have co-authored for feedback and discussion. Specifically, I trace the connection between my interests in substantive theoretical and content areas to my recent work on multiverse analysis, a research tool that can help reconcile variability in empirical results by systematically testing competing rationales against each other and thus, facilitate both knowledge aggregation and theory building. I then offer two early-stage projects for feedback on my attempts to offer methodological extensions of multiverse analyses in the context of my substantive interest in theorizing and studying how Chief Executive Officers (CEOs) affect organizations.

title: Global Family Cafe
description:
Global Family Cafe is a welcoming space for everyone, including F2 and J2 spouses and families of all ages.  Join us in a warm, intercultural environment where family members can gather and share their cultures and experiences in conversation. These gatherings are offered weekly only in the fall and spring semesters. Registration is not required. You are welcome to attend anytime!

A collaboration between International Christian Fellowship (ICF) and Intercultural Programs (ICP).

 

Be Globally Engaged!

 

Disclaimer: The University of Texas at Dallas Intercultural Programs and International Christian Fellowship will not take custodial responsibility of minors while participating in Global Family Cafe. Custodial responsibility will remain with teachers K-12, parents, legal guardians, and chaperones.

title: UCC: JP Morgan Chase, Info Session
description:
Interested in a career at the intersection of finance, business strategy, and data analysis? Join J.P. Morgan Chase for an information session about their Global Finance and Business Management Analyst Program!

During this session, representatives will provide insights into the program, share what it’s like to work within one of the world’s leading financial institutions, and discuss the skills and experiences that can set you apart in the selection process.

Who Should Attend:
This event is open to all majors, with a particular emphasis on students who have skills or interest in:

  • Excel and data analysis
  • Creative problem-solving and critical thinking
  • Finance, project management, treasury, data analytics and more

Eligibility:
The program is targeted toward students graduating in December 2026 or May 2027 (current sophomores and juniors).

If you’re an analytical thinker looking to gain hands-on experience in a dynamic, global organization—this is your opportunity to learn more and connect directly with J.P. Morgan Chase!

 

Photography and video recording may occur at this event. By attending, you consent to being photographed and recorded for use by UT Dallas in promotional materials, social media, and university publications.

title: Tea Table Talks Support Group
description:
“Sharing tea with a fascinating stranger is one of life’s greatest treasures.” – Uncle Iroh from ATLA

Tea Table Talks is a general mental health support group for students to share life’s highs and lows. Whether you're feeling overwhelmed, isolated, or just craving real connection, this group is a place to be seen, heard, and supported. We will have tea and conversations steeped in support. 
 

To join, simply come to SSB 4.600 a few minutes before the meeting time. If you’d like reminders and an easier check-in, you can also message us at sccgroups@utdallas.edu to be added to the roster.

These groups provide an opportunity for support from others who hold similar identities or life experiences. Participation is open and drop-in style, meaning members do not have to be current clients of the Student Counseling Center, and you may attend meetings as often or as seldom as you like. Support groups are open to all UTD students, and no group screening is required. Please note support groups are not the same as therapy groups in that they are more focused on building community and peer support guided by one of our therapists than in-depth therapeutic intervention.

Tea Table Talks is a general mental health support group for students to share life’s highs and lows. Whether you're feeling overwhelmed, isolated, or just craving real connection, this group is a place to be seen, heard, and supported. We will have tea and conversations steeped in support. 
 

To join, simply come to SSB 4.600 a few minutes before the meeting time. If you’d like reminders and an easier check-in, you can also message us at sccgroups@utdallas.edu to be added to the roster.

These groups provide an opportunity for support from others who hold similar identities or life experiences. Participation is open and drop-in style, meaning members do not have to be current clients of the Student Counseling Center, and you may attend meetings as often or as seldom as you like. Support groups are open to all UTD students, and no group screening is required. Please note support groups are not the same as therapy groups in that they are more focused on building community and peer support guided by one of our therapists than in-depth therapeutic intervention.

title: SCC & CSR's Find Us Fridays
description:
Treat yourself at the end of the week with a cup of coffee or fidgets, and explore the recreational resources available in the Center for Students in Recovery’s lounge and the Student Counseling Center's Calming Corner! Students can enjoy some coloring, play board games, work on a puzzle — and even try out the CSR's Wii! Feel free to hop between both spaces.

'Find Us Fridays' will take place weekly on Fridays this spring semester from 1:00pm-3:00pm in SSB 4.500 and SSB 4.602.

For any questions, please email recovery@utdallas.edu or counselingcenter@utdallas.edu.

title: iWeek: Global Talent Show
description:
Experience campus global presence through song, dance and more. The last event of UT Dallas' annual International Week (iWeek), the Global Talent Show is an exciting way to celebrate the global plurality of UT Dallas. This program includes the announcement of winners from Passport to the World. It is a show you won't want to miss.

In special collaboration this year with UT Dallas Alumni, Comets Giving Days bonus funds will be awarded to 1st, 2nd, and 3rd place winners. Prior to the event, stop by the SSA lobby to meet with the UT Dallas Alumni team and pick up your Comes Giving Days giveaways!

Doors will open at 6:30 p.m. Seating is available on a first come, first served basis. Brought to you by Intercultural Programs, cultural student organizations, and UT Dallas Alumni.

Be Globally Engaged!

Photo by Hulki Okan Tabak via Unsplashed.

title: Collegiate Recovery Week's Dimension Days: Community
description:
Join the Center for Students in Recovery, the Student Organization Center, Fraternity Sorority Life, S.T.A.R.S, and Universal Recreation as we take part in recognizing Collegiate Recovery Week by exploring one of the four dimensions of recovery - community. SAMHSA (Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration) defines community in life in recovery as relationships and social networks that provide support, friendship, love, and hope.

Students will have the chance to receive a a giveaway tote bag filled with small goodies by visiting each department's table (while supplies last). During this event students will also get to play board games, puzzle, and make their own bracelets!

The event will take place on Thursday, April 16th from 1:00pm – 3:00pm at the first floor of the Student Union (by the pool tables).
No registration required. For any questions, please contact recovery@utdallas.edu.

We hope to see you there!

title: Polykarp Kusch Lecture Series | Repairing Damaged Brain Circuits: A 25-Year Journey from Lab to FDA Approval.
description:
The Polykarp Kusch Lecture Series: Concerns of the Lively Mind continues with this year's honoree, Dr. Michael Kilgard, Margaret Fonde Jonsson Professor of Neuroscience. Dr. Kilgard will be delivering his lecture at 2pm on April 22nd in the SSA Auditorium. All guests, on and off campus, are welcome to attend.

Lecture Details:

Repairing Damaged Brain Circuits: A 25-Year Journey from Lab to FDA Approval.
An examination of how responses to public problems are shaped by historical and cultural context, by the professional and ideological perspectives of decisionmakers, and by assumptions about what actions are considered to be legitimate and illegitimate and whose participation in the decision process is considered to be appropriate. Illustrations will be provided from social science research and from contemporary policy dilemmas.

title: In Conversation with Gajin Fujita
description:
Join us for a moderated conversation between exhibition curator, Delwyn Davis, and featured artist Gajin Fujita, whose work is on view in Paper Knife: Objects of Beauty in Early Modern Japan. Moving from the historical realities of the samurai class to its mythologized presence in contemporary American imagination, the discussion will consider how Fujita draws on Japanese visual traditions such as ukiyo-e prints, gold-leaf screens, and warrior iconography while merging them with the language of graffiti, pop culture, and urban Los Angeles. Together, Davis and Fujita will reflect on the curatorial strategy of placing Fujita’s work in dialogue with objects from the Crow collection, examining how history, identity, and the Western gaze shape evolving interpretations of the samurai today.

The conversation will also address Fujita’s process, materials, and personal history, including intergenerational influence and the blending of craft and street practice. Audience members will gain deeper insight into how historical narratives are reframed through contemporary art, and how the samurai endures as both cultural symbol and evolving myth.

Come early for a happy hour beginning at 5:00 pm, prior to the conversation.

Free and open to the public. Advanced registration is encouraged.

Crow Museum of Asian Art in the Downtown Dallas Arts District
2010 Flora St., Dallas, TX, 75201

Register

Parking: Attendees can park in the Trammell Crow Center garage for two hours and get their tickets validated by the front desk.

Image: Gajin Fujita, Demon Slayer, 2015, spray paint, paint markers, Mean Streak, 12k white gold, 24k gold and platinum leaf on wood panels

title: JSOM Global Service Week
description:
Come join us for UTDserv’s Week of Service in celebration of National Volunteer Week! This is your chance to get involved, give back, and make a real difference across the Dallas–Fort Worth community. From hands-on service projects to meaningful partnerships with local nonprofits, there’s an opportunity for everyone.

This year, JSOM Global Service Week, in collaboration with JSOM Abroad, highlights how local action creates global impact—supporting organizations that serve international and refugee communities right here in North Texas.

✨ Earn volunteer hours
🌎 Support impactful causes
🚀 Build leadership and service skills

Bring your friends, pick a project that fits your schedule, and come make an impact with us—spots are limited, so sign up today!

title: Fast Track in MS Marketing Information Session
description:
Do you have questions about the Fast Track in MS Marketing?

The Fast-Track for the Master’s in Marketing program allows undergraduate students at The University of Texas at Dallas to begin work on their MS in Marketing before graduation. Qualified juniors and seniors may take up to 12 credits of graduate coursework in marketing that will apply toward the Bachelor of Science degree as well as satisfy requirements for the Master’s in Marketing. 

Fast Track lets you save both time and money and potentially earn both your BS and MS degrees in five years or less.

This is your chance to learn more about how the Fast Track program works and ask any questions that you might have. 

For more information, please visit this web page:  https://marketing.utdallas.edu/program-resources/fast-track/

title: Resonance: From Archive to Art
description:
Resonance: From Archive to Art is a public program that brings together video art, performance, oral history, and dialogue to explore how historical archives and lived memories can be translated into contemporary artistic forms.

Presented by the Asian American Art and Culture Initiative (AAACI) in celebration of America's 250th Anniversary and Asian American & Pacific Islander Heritage Month, Resonance draws on archival research from the Houston Asian American Archive and Austin History Center to explore the lives of pioneering Asian Texans Joe Lung and Inez Lung Lee through experimental video, live performance, artist dialogue, and their descendants.

As part of their tour, the Center for Asian Studies at UT Dallas is proud to serve as the Dallas host! Be on the lookout for more details and information as the event nears!

title: José Bowen
description:
José Antonio Bowen has performed in 46 states and 17 countries and with Stan Getz, Dizzy Gillespie, Bobby McFerrin, Dave Brubeck, Liberace, and many other musical luminaries. 

At this concert at UT Dallas, Dr. Bowen returns with his sextet, including Chris Milyo (saxophone) & Peter Clagett (trumpet) and new original composistions and new arrangements of jazz standards. 

Get connected. Join the Bass School mailing list.

title: Canceled: Marina Dichenko & Mikhail Berestnev in Recital: Music for Violin and Piano by Medtner, Stravinsky & Prokofiev
description:
Due to unforseen circumstances our recital with Marina Dichenko on the 18th of April is cancelled.

Violinist Marina Dichenko and pianist Mikhail Berestnev return to the stage presenting Igor Stravinsky's "Suite ltalienne," arranged by famed violinist Samuel Dushkin, and the rarely performed Sonata for Violin and Piano #1 by Nikolai Medtner. 

                                                       Program:

Nikolai Medtner – Sonata for violin and piano #1 in B Minor op. 21

  • Canzona
  • Danza
  • Ditirambo

 

Igor Stravinsky – Suite Italienne

  • Introduzione
  • Serenata
  • Tarantella
  • Gavotte con Due Variazioni
  • Scherzino
  • Minuetto e Finale

                                                  Intermission

Sergei Prokofiev – Sonata for violin and piano #2 in D Major, op. 94a

  • Moderato
  • Presto
  • Andante
  • Allegro con Brio

                                                            

Get connected. Join the Bass School mailing list.

Parking Information:

Use Google Maps to navigate to Parking Structure 3 (PS3) and park in a Gold or Orange space.

Once parked, visit our Venues page to obtain turn-by-turn walking directions to Jonsson Performance Hall. If you'd like to avoid using the interactive campus map, simply walk south from PS3 and turn left when you see Jonsson Academic Center (JO).

Enter the doors on the west side of the building and continue straight toward the elevators. The floor you enter the building on is floor 3, walk down hallway towards the elevators and take the stairs to your left - you will arrive at the Jonsson Performance Hall (The elevators will not take you to the PH).

title: Preservation Week-Oral Histories
description: The most important stories are often the ones never written down. Join Special Collections and Archives staff in the McDermott Library Lobby to celebrate Preservation Week with a conversation about oral histories. Find out what they are, how to make them, and the voices already preserved in our collections. Pick up a free oral history zine and discover how easy it is to start preserving your own story.

title: EPPS-American Airlines Data Challenge Competition
description:
Are you ready to tackle a real-world problem using your data analytics and AI skills?

Join the EPPS–American Airlines Data Challenge Competition, co-hosted by UTD EPPS and the American Airlines Operations Research & Advanced Analytics Team. This exciting competition gives you the opportunity to solve an authentic industry problem directly provided by American Airlines.

Who can apply?

  • Teams of 2–5 undergraduate or graduate students
  • Must be currently enrolled at UTD
  • Interdisciplinary teams are encouraged

Important Dates:

  • RSVP Deadline: April 7 - RSVP LINK: https://utd.link/3r3
  • Challenge Released: April 8
  • Final Report Due: April 22
  • Showcase Presentations: April 24 (2:00–3:30 PM, GR 3.420)
    • All EPPS TAs are required to attend this event and serve as a judge.

Competition Highlights:

  • Work on a real operational challenge from a leading global airline
  • Present your solution to industry professionals and data science experts
  • Top-scoring teams will be invited to present at the Showcase Event on April 24
  • Awards and prizes will be presented to the best-performing teams

Parking for the Theatre:

If you'd like to avoid using the interactive campus map, simply walk south from PS3 and turn left before you reach Jonsson Academic Center (JO). This route avoids stairs. If you turn after you've walked past JO, you'll need to walk down the stairs along the side of the building.

The entrance to University Theatre is on the east side of JO and faces east. There are picnic tables in front of the entrance.

title: URSA 2026 Semifinal Poster Contest
description:
Current recipients of the Undergraduate Research Scholar Awards discuss their research with event attendees, utilizing a research poster and their in-person research presentation skills. Research faculty members judge and select the strongest projects representing each academic school.

Public presentation of research through poster presentations is an important component of an undergraduate student’s research journey. All research disciplines and undergraduate academic groups are represented during the symposium, and participants enjoy the opportunity to speak in-person to members of the internal and external UT Dallas community about the significance of their work.

title: Welcome In Wednesdays @ Basic Needs Resource Center
description:
Welcome In Wednesdays are a weekly event for Comets to visit the Basic Needs Resource Center (BNRC) and learn about our resources and services! Everyone is invited to visit the BNRC lounge to relax, socialize, study, play board games or Nintendo Switch, visit Temoc’s Closet, and learn about the newest office in the Health and Wellness Initiatives in Student Affairs! Stop by each Wednesday from 10 a.m.- 4 p.m.

On select Welcome In Wednesdays, from 2 p.m.- 3 p.m. in the SSB 4.300 lounge, the BNRC invites on-campus departments, student organizations, and community partners to host workshops and events to support students' health and wellness. Spring 2026 calendar to be announced!

---

For more information about the BNRC, please follow us on Instagram @utdbasicneeds. Please reach out to our team via email with any questions at basicneeds@utdallas.edu.

title: Refill Roundup
description:
Participants will visit a list of designated refill stations across campus and record the number of bottle refills shown on each station’s counter. This simple data helps us understand how often refill stations are used, identify high‑impact locations, and support future water conservation efforts.

You will be sent a form to fill out via email associated with the shift's listed locations. Please only fill out the locations assigned to your shift. After your list's locations is completed, you may reply back to Sustainability@UTDallas.edu on the same email to notify the team that you have completed your list. Upon verification of data submitted for your assigned locations, you will be awarded 1 Impact Hour.

Bring a phone or another mobile device, comfortable shoes, and your reusable water bottle if you have one. It’s an easy, hands‑on way to contribute to sustainability while exploring campus and learning how small actions like refilling can make a big difference!

title: Groundbreakers: Post-War Japan and Korea from the DMA Collection
description:
September 6, 2025 - July 26, 2026

Groundbreakers brings together artists who played with materiality, space, and performance in postwar Japan and Korea after the 1950s. Moving beyond the hand, some artists used unexpected parts of their bodies to make their marks: Shiraga painted with his feet and Matsutani used his mouth to create vinyl bubbles. By extension, their bodily performances became part of their art. The objects and paintings themselves are testaments to the ephemeral nature of their energetic performance.

Other artists of this period upended the implement of the brush by pouring directly onto the canvas or experimented further with materiality by using different mediums, such as tin. Proponents of three art movements—Mono-ha, Dansaekhwa, and Gutai—rigorously interrogated and explored artistic performances, playful use of materials, experimentations with new techniques, a commitment to direct gestures, and a reorientation of subject and object. Through it all, the very process and stages of presenting objects became as important as the final art form.

A common visual thread amongst these artists is a commitment to abstraction and minimalism. These art forms of painting, sound, and installation are meant to be participatory, expanding how the viewer interacts with works of art. Challenging traditional ideas of art, each object is a transformative site that discourages passive looking. In the case of Takamatsu’s Cube 6 + 3, which greets visitors at the entrance of the exhibition, the artist’s simple application of lines onto a three-dimensional cube alters our perception of space and depth.

Two contemporary artists, Tatsuo Miyajima and Do Ho Suh, are positioned as means to provoke a dialogue and conversation about the antecedents and legacy of performance art for contemporary artists and its twin accompaniment the viewer/participant.

This exhibition is organized by The University of Texas at Dallas in collaboration with The Dallas Museum of Art.

On view at the Edith and Peter O'Donnell Jr. Athenaeum.

Athenaeum hours: 11 a.m. to 5 p.m. Tuesday through Sunday. Free admission.

title: Navigating Sites and Spaces: Reclaiming Agency through Material, Movement, and Media
description:
Navigating Sites and Spaces: Reclaiming Agency through Material, Movement, and Media

Parul Bhatia MFA Thesis Exhibition

This MFA thesis exhibition presents an immersive, multimedia installation exploring absence, memory, and self-autonomy through material, movement, and media. Working across performance, photography, video, material installations, and sculptural forms, the exhibition examines how bodily gestures, material imprints, and encounters with space function as sites of transformation. Drawing from personal memory, ritual, and ecological relationships, the work invites viewers into a contemplative environment where presence and absence coexist, and where material processes become pathways for reclaiming agency and belonging.

Parul Bhatia’s MFA thesis exhibition at SP/N Gallery has been supported in part by Center for Asian Studies at The University of Texas at Dallas.

title: Organic Worlds: Symbiogenesis in Art
description:
Organic Worlds: Symbiogenesis in Art

Feb. 7- April 28, 2026

SP/N Gallery

University of Texas at Dallas

https://bass.utdallas.edu/spn-gallery/

 

            Biology is more than genes, pharmaceuticals, and natural selection. Before any of these, biology is historical, modeled by where, when, and how it is written, bearing the legible marks of a cultural moment like rings on a tree or plaque on a tooth. Every quality of biology is thus situated in time and circumstance. Genes function properly inside of cells; drugs are profit engines for pharmaceutical companies; and natural selection is one circle of selective activity among others operating within earth’s atmosphere. So, life is almost always coupled to other life. It is symbiotic. Symbiogenesis is the leading theory of evolution, which is based on symbiotic cooperation between microbes occurring millions of years ago, as mitochondria and chloroplasts, organelles essential to the metabolism of animal and plant cells, bear the DNA of once free-ranging microbes.

Organic Worlds: Symbiogenesis in Art is an exhibition of art about biology understood from the perspective of context, collaboration, and coupling. It focuses on biological symbiosis in the artwork of Amy Youngs and Ken Rinaldo, setting in relief the significant role non-scientists play in writing biology. Exhibition artworks include two-dimensional works and time-based media that involve sound, touch, smell, immersion, amplification, and magnification.

Ken Rinaldo is internationally recognized for interactive AI bio-robotic art installations. He creates hybrid ecologies that integrate humans, machines, plants, animals, and more-than-human others, exploring idealized social and biological symbioses. Amy M. Youngs creates eco art, interactive sculptures, and digital media works that explore entanglements between technology, plants, and animals. Her interdisciplinary research involves empathy, relationships with non-humans, ecosystem construction, and seeing through the eyes of machines.

 

--Charissa N. Terranova, Curator of Organic Worlds: Symbiogenesis in Art and Margaret M. McDermott Distinguished Chair in Art and Aesthetic Studies at the Harry W. Bass Jr. School of Arts, Humanities, and Technology, University of Texas at Dallas

Genes function properly inside of cells; drugs are profit engines for pharmaceutical companies; and natural selection is one circle of selective activity among others operating within earth’s atmosphere. So, life is almost always coupled to other life. It is symbiotic. Symbiogenesis is the leading theory of evolution, which is based on symbiotic cooperation between microbes occurring millions of years ago, as mitochondria and chloroplasts, organelles essential to the metabolism of animal and plant cells, bear the DNA of once free-ranging microbes.

Organic Worlds: Symbiogenesis in Art is an exhibition of art about biology understood from the perspective of context, collaboration, and coupling. It focuses on biological symbiosis in the artwork of Amy Youngs and Ken Rinaldo, setting in relief the significant role non-scientists play in writing biology. Exhibition artworks include two-dimensional works and time-based media that involve sound, touch, smell, immersion, amplification, and magnification.

Ken Rinaldo is internationally recognized for interactive AI bio-robotic art installations. He creates hybrid ecologies that integrate humans, machines, plants, animals, and more-than-human others, exploring idealized social and biological symbioses. Amy M. Youngs creates eco art, interactive sculptures, and digital media works that explore entanglements between technology, plants, and animals. Her interdisciplinary research involves empathy, relationships with non-humans, ecosystem construction, and seeing through the eyes of machines.

 

--Charissa N. Terranova, Curator of Organic Worlds: Symbiogenesis in Art and Margaret M. McDermott Distinguished Chair in Art and Aesthetic Studies at the Harry W. Bass Jr. School of Arts, Humanities, and Technology, University of Texas at Dallas

title: Homecoming : A Capstone Performance by Bex
description:
Bex is exhausted. A solo performer, she finds herself weighed down by the expectations and desires she thinks she should have. After years of silent despair, she decides to break free. Through destroying the life she worked so hard to build for herself, she learns to rise from the ashes of herself and write her own story.

Performed with members of the Anime Orchestra Ensemble, Homecoming grapples with self-identity and acceptance through music and animation. Featuring songs from various Japanese media and an original piece composed by Bex herself, this performance takes the audience on a journey through both the grief and the joy experienced through transformation.

title: Groundbreakers: Post-War Japan and Korea from the DMA Collection
description:
September 6, 2025 - July 26, 2026

Groundbreakers brings together artists who played with materiality, space, and performance in postwar Japan and Korea after the 1950s. Moving beyond the hand, some artists used unexpected parts of their bodies to make their marks: Shiraga painted with his feet and Matsutani used his mouth to create vinyl bubbles. By extension, their bodily performances became part of their art. The objects and paintings themselves are testaments to the ephemeral nature of their energetic performance.

Other artists of this period upended the implement of the brush by pouring directly onto the canvas or experimented further with materiality by using different mediums, such as tin. Proponents of three art movements—Mono-ha, Dansaekhwa, and Gutai—rigorously interrogated and explored artistic performances, playful use of materials, experimentations with new techniques, a commitment to direct gestures, and a reorientation of subject and object. Through it all, the very process and stages of presenting objects became as important as the final art form.

A common visual thread amongst these artists is a commitment to abstraction and minimalism. These art forms of painting, sound, and installation are meant to be participatory, expanding how the viewer interacts with works of art. Challenging traditional ideas of art, each object is a transformative site that discourages passive looking. In the case of Takamatsu’s Cube 6 + 3, which greets visitors at the entrance of the exhibition, the artist’s simple application of lines onto a three-dimensional cube alters our perception of space and depth.

Two contemporary artists, Tatsuo Miyajima and Do Ho Suh, are positioned as means to provoke a dialogue and conversation about the antecedents and legacy of performance art for contemporary artists and its twin accompaniment the viewer/participant.

This exhibition is organized by The University of Texas at Dallas in collaboration with The Dallas Museum of Art.

On view at the Edith and Peter O'Donnell Jr. Athenaeum.

Athenaeum hours: 11 a.m. to 5 p.m. Tuesday through Sunday. Free admission.

title: Learning to Heal: Trauma Processing Group
description:
We are collecting interest to choose a time/date for this semester. If you are interested, please reach out to sccgroups@utdallas.edu with your availability, and group will begin once we have enough students and a time/day is chosen.

Learning to Heal from Trauma will introduce students to the impacts of trauma and to topics such as boundaries, power and control, healthy relationships, and self-compassion. From these topics, the group members will explore their own patterns of responding to trauma and begin to establish new ways of coping and begin/continue their process of healing.

Process groups are focused on the exploration and open processing and discussion of participants. Process groups are led by one of our therapists and typically more open-ended and less structured around a specific lesson or topic for the day. Clients are required to complete a group screening to assess whether the group matches their needs and interest.

For process groups, if you are not a current or recent client, please make an appointment to get started and note your interest in group therapy. You’ll complete intake paperwork and have a 30-minute “IC” (individual consultation) with one of our therapists, and then get scheduled for a brief screening meeting with the group’s leader.

If you are a current or recent client, reach out to our Groups & Workshops Coordinator at sccgroups@utdallas.edu to schedule a screening meeting.

title: OUTer Space - LGBTQ+ Support Group (Undergraduate Students)
description:
We are collecting interest to choose a time/date for this semester. If you are interested, please reach out to sccgroups@utdallas.edu with your availability, and group will begin once we have enough students and a time/day is chosen.

Drop-in mental health support group for LGBTQIA+ undergraduate students who want to talk about validating and supporting others and themselves.

These groups provide an opportunity for support from others who hold similar identities or life experiences. Participation is open and drop-in style, meaning members do not have to be current clients of the Student Counseling Center, and you may attend meetings as often or as seldom as you like. Support groups are open to all UTD students, and no group screening is required. Please note support groups are not the same as therapy groups in that they are more focused on building community and peer support guided by one of our therapists than in-depth therapeutic intervention.

title: S.T.A.R.S. – Supportive Tabletop Alliance for Recreation and Socialization
description:
Join us for a growing initiative from the UTD Student Counseling Center: the S.T.A.R.S. (Supportive Tabletop Alliance for Recreation and Socialization) gaming community! Since Spring 2025, we have been offering students the chance to join in fun, connection, and adventure through the world of Dungeons & Dragons and other tabletop role-playing games.

We have multiple groups running through the semester in a wide variety of times and days!

Students: Are you ready to become part of a team and embark on epic adventures with your fellow students? Through S.T.A.R.S., we have created a safe, supportive space for students to explore new identities, share experiences and have fun together without any pressure or agenda. No, this isn’t a sneaky therapy session! It’s all about building community through fun.

Faculty and Staff: We’re seeking staff and faculty members who are interested in volunteering as Dungeon Masters to lead our game campaigns. title: SPARK Femmes (Sex and Pornography Addiction Recovery Kit) #3
description:
We are collecting interest to choose a time/date for this semester. If you are interested, please reach out to sccgroups@utdallas.edu with your availability, and group will begin once we have enough students and a time/day is chosen.

SPARK Femmes is a supportive and nonjudgmental meeting place for woman/femmes who are questioning or struggling with the ways they engage with sex and/or pornography. This group will hold space for students to process their concerns, define healthy sex for themselves, and build tools to help navigate distress. Whether this is an issue that’s recently come up or is something you have navigated for a long time, this group can help meet you where you are.

Process groups are focused on the exploration and open processing and discussion of participants. Process groups are led by one of our therapists and typically more open-ended and less structured around a specific lesson or topic for the day. Clients are required to complete a group screening to assess whether the group matches their needs and interest.

For process groups, if you are not a current or recent client, please make an appointment to get started and note your interest in group therapy. You’ll complete intake paperwork and have a 30-minute “IC” (individual consultation) with one of our therapists, and then get scheduled for a brief screening meeting with the group’s leader.

If you are a current or recent client, reach out to our Groups & Workshops Coordinator at sccgroups@utdallas.edu to schedule a screening meeting.

title: Sustainability Stewards Training
description:
The Office of Sustainability encourages current students, staff, and faculty to participate in a free Sustainability Stewards certification. This virtual certification is an overview of basic sustainability principles, sustainability on campus, and more. Participants are encouraged to ask questions, interact with the course content, and participate in a short, voluntary checks for understanding throughout each training session.

At the end of this training, participants will receive the Sustainability Steward designation, certifying that they understand basic principles and concepts of sustainability at UTD, as well as a certificate and a Sustainability Steward sticker to display. For more information, please subscribe to the Sustainability Newsletter to get future dates and announcements.

title: Digital Accessibility Office Hours
description:
State and federal law requires that the University's digital communications be accessible to all users, including people with disabilities. Accessibility standards apply to websites; PDF, Word and PowerPoint documents; course content; videos and podcasts; social media posts; and more. Federal regulations require that UT Dallas' digital communications meet WCAG 2.1 AA standards by April 24, 2026. Learn more about digital accessibility.

UTD staff and faculty who are looking to assess accessibility of content or dive deeper into particular accessibility challenges are invited to join digital accessibility office hours on Teams. This session will be hosted by Christy Grant, director of web accessibility in the Office of Communications and Marketing. This is a drop-in session. Bring your accessibility questions or content you want to have reviewed. 

Join the meeting. Registration not required.

title: Relationship Roadmap Workshop
description:
Group will begin soon - once enough students are signed up!

This 7-week hybrid in-person and virtual workshop is designed for college students looking to strengthen their romantic relationships. Based on Dr. John Gottman’s The Seven Principles for Making Marriage Work, the workshop offers practical tools and evidence-based strategies tailored to the unique challenges faced in the context of college relationships. Each week, participants will explore a principle and learn skills to improve communication, manage conflict, build trust, and deepen connection – all in an engaging and supportive environment.

Whether you’re dating, engaged, in a long-term partnership, or looking to build important relationship skills for the future, this workshop provides a solid foundation for creating a healthy and lasting relationship during your college years and beyond. This workshop is affirming and inclusive of all types of relationships, LGBTQ+, and polyamory. People in relationships are welcome to attend together!


To join, simply click the Comet Calendar link or come to SSB 4.600 a few minutes before the start time. If you’d like reminders and an easier check-in, you can also message us at sccgroups@utdallas.edu to be added to the roster.

Our workshops provide education and practical tools for managing common mental health concerns, similar to a training or class. Even though they are led by one of our therapists, workshops are not the same as therapy groups, as they are focused on learning and practicing skills rather than in-depth therapeutic process. All workshops are open to UTD students, and no group screening is required.

title: DBT-U (Dialectical Behavioral Therapy for University Students)
description:
Group will begin soon - once enough students are signed up!

DBT-U is an open, eight-week, hybrid process- and skills-based group for students to learn and develop coping skills and strategies to improve individual functioning. This group is specifically for clients who have difficulties in emotion regulation, interpersonal difficulties, and pattern of crisis. Group members learn topics related to mindfulness skills, interpersonal effectiveness and communication strategies, emotion regulation, and distress tolerance skills in a structured and supportive learning environment. Each group consists of a brief mindfulness exercise, check-in/introductions, introduction of new skills, discussion/experiential practice and assignment of practice exercise and check-out.

Hybrid skills/process groups are focused on the exploration and open processing and discussion of participants. Hybrid skills/process groups are led by one of our therapists and typically more open-ended and less structured around a specific lesson or topic for the day, though new skills and strategies are often a topic of discussion. Clients are required to complete a group screening to assess whether the group matches their needs and interest.

For Hybrid skills/process groups, if you are not a current or recent client, please make an appointment to get started and note your interest in group therapy. You’ll complete intake paperwork and have a 30-minute “IC” (individual consultation) with one of our therapists, and then get scheduled for a brief screening meeting with the group’s leader.

If you are a current or recent client, reach out to our Groups & Workshops Coordinator at sccgroups@utdallas.edu to schedule a screening meeting.

title: Graduate Student Support Group
description:
Join us to discuss - challenges of being a graduate student, fears about immigration, imposter syndrome, loneliness, motivation, managing relationships with faculty, work-life balance, & more! This is a relaxed support space to connect with other graduate students, get some mental health tips, and share resources on and around campus.

To join, simply click the Comet Calendar link at the start time. If you’d like reminders and an easier check-in, you can also message us at sccgroups@utdallas.edu to be added to the roster.

These groups provide an opportunity for support from others who hold similar identities or life experiences. Participation is open and drop-in style, meaning members do not have to be current clients of the Student Counseling Center, and you may attend meetings as often or as seldom as you like. Support groups are open to all UTD students, and no group screening is required. Please note support groups are not the same as therapy groups in that they are more focused on building community and peer support guided by one of our therapists than in-depth therapeutic intervention.

title: Graduate Studies Annual Alumni Speakers Series Event - Lily George and Mya Adams
description:
Listen to advice and guidance from alumni from the History Masters program: Lily George and Mya Adams.

Lily George
Lily earned her undergraduate degree in History from UT Dallas and completed her master's in History through the UTD Fast Track program. After working as an Academic Advisor at UTD's ECS Advising office, she currently serves as Historical Marker Program Specialist and Office Manager for the History Programs Division at the Texas Historical Commission headquarters in Austin.
 
Mya Adams
Mya Renee Adams is a Photographs Cataloguer at Heritage Auctions, where she has worked for four years, specializing in the research, cataloging, and preparation of thousands of photographs annually for auction. She earned her B.A. in Visual and Performing Arts (Art History concentration) from The University of Texas at Dallas in 2020 and was the first to complete the Edith O’Donnell Institute of Art History (EODIAH) Fast Track program in 2021. Born and raised on O'ahu, Hawai‘i, her master’s thesis, Staged Island Narratives: A Comparative Analysis of Three Non-Native Artists Working in 1930s Hawai‘i, reflects a culture, art, and history she is deeply passionate about. Mya relocated to Dallas in 2016 and has since held research and arts administration roles at the Dallas Museum of Art and the Dallas Art Fair. She is an aspiring auctioneer with a strong interest in the intersection of scholarship and the art market.

title: Groundbreakers: Post-War Japan and Korea from the DMA Collection
description:
September 6, 2025 - July 26, 2026

Groundbreakers brings together artists who played with materiality, space, and performance in postwar Japan and Korea after the 1950s. Moving beyond the hand, some artists used unexpected parts of their bodies to make their marks: Shiraga painted with his feet and Matsutani used his mouth to create vinyl bubbles. By extension, their bodily performances became part of their art. The objects and paintings themselves are testaments to the ephemeral nature of their energetic performance.

Other artists of this period upended the implement of the brush by pouring directly onto the canvas or experimented further with materiality by using different mediums, such as tin. Proponents of three art movements—Mono-ha, Dansaekhwa, and Gutai—rigorously interrogated and explored artistic performances, playful use of materials, experimentations with new techniques, a commitment to direct gestures, and a reorientation of subject and object. Through it all, the very process and stages of presenting objects became as important as the final art form.

A common visual thread amongst these artists is a commitment to abstraction and minimalism. These art forms of painting, sound, and installation are meant to be participatory, expanding how the viewer interacts with works of art. Challenging traditional ideas of art, each object is a transformative site that discourages passive looking. In the case of Takamatsu’s Cube 6 + 3, which greets visitors at the entrance of the exhibition, the artist’s simple application of lines onto a three-dimensional cube alters our perception of space and depth.

Two contemporary artists, Tatsuo Miyajima and Do Ho Suh, are positioned as means to provoke a dialogue and conversation about the antecedents and legacy of performance art for contemporary artists and its twin accompaniment the viewer/participant.

This exhibition is organized by The University of Texas at Dallas in collaboration with The Dallas Museum of Art.

On view at the Edith and Peter O'Donnell Jr. Athenaeum.

Athenaeum hours: 11 a.m. to 5 p.m. Tuesday through Sunday. Free admission.

title: Learning to Heal: Trauma Processing Group
description:
We are collecting interest to choose a time/date for this semester. If you are interested, please reach out to sccgroups@utdallas.edu with your availability, and group will begin once we have enough students and a time/day is chosen.

Learning to Heal from Trauma will introduce students to the impacts of trauma and to topics such as boundaries, power and control, healthy relationships, and self-compassion. From these topics, the group members will explore their own patterns of responding to trauma and begin to establish new ways of coping and begin/continue their process of healing.

Process groups are focused on the exploration and open processing and discussion of participants. Process groups are led by one of our therapists and typically more open-ended and less structured around a specific lesson or topic for the day. Clients are required to complete a group screening to assess whether the group matches their needs and interest.

For process groups, if you are not a current or recent client, please make an appointment to get started and note your interest in group therapy. You’ll complete intake paperwork and have a 30-minute “IC” (individual consultation) with one of our therapists, and then get scheduled for a brief screening meeting with the group’s leader.

If you are a current or recent client, reach out to our Groups & Workshops Coordinator at sccgroups@utdallas.edu to schedule a screening meeting.

title: S.T.A.R.S. – Supportive Tabletop Alliance for Recreation and Socialization
description:
Join us for a growing initiative from the UTD Student Counseling Center: the S.T.A.R.S. (Supportive Tabletop Alliance for Recreation and Socialization) gaming community! Since Spring 2025, we have been offering students the chance to join in fun, connection, and adventure through the world of Dungeons & Dragons and other tabletop role-playing games.

We have multiple groups running through the semester in a wide variety of times and days!

Students: Are you ready to become part of a team and embark on epic adventures with your fellow students? Through S.T.A.R.S., we have created a safe, supportive space for students to explore new identities, share experiences and have fun together without any pressure or agenda. No, this isn’t a sneaky therapy session! It’s all about building community through fun.

Faculty and Staff: We’re seeking staff and faculty members who are interested in volunteering as Dungeon Masters to lead our game campaigns. No prior experience is required - just a passion for storytelling and a willingness to help create a fun and inclusive experience. The Student Counseling Center will provide all the training and orientation you need to lead the adventures!

If you’re interested in joining, we encourage you to fill out this brief survey to share your availability and help grow and shape this exciting new community.

Survey Link: https://utd.link/STARS 

If you’d like to get involved or have any questions, please reach out to us at supportivegamers@utdallas.edu.

description:
April is Stress Awareness Month: Learn to calm your body when you feel stressed.

Stress is something we all experience, but when left unaddressed, it can take a real toll on our mental and physical health. That's why this month matters: it's an opportunity to start honest conversations, reduce stigma, and prioritize our wellbeing. The LearnToLive program can help members develop healthier habits, boundary-setting techniques, and stress management strategies.

Register for a LearnToLive webinar to help manage stress by clicking on a link below and entering the access code: BETTERME.

Managing Stress and Worry
Wednesday, April 8th: 12-12:30pm CT

When Substance Use Becomes a Concern
Tuesday, April 14th: 11-11:30am CT

The Price of Silence: How to Talk about Mental Health
Friday, April 17th: 10-10:30am CT

Promoting More Helpful Self-Talk
Wednesday, April 22nd: 2-2:30pm CT

Engaging Your 5 Senses to Reduce Stress

title: Navigating Sites and Spaces: Reclaiming Agency through Material, Movement, and Media
description:
Navigating Sites and Spaces: Reclaiming Agency through Material, Movement, and Media

Parul Bhatia MFA Thesis Exhibition

This MFA thesis exhibition presents an immersive, multimedia installation exploring absence, memory, and self-autonomy through material, movement, and media. Working across performance, photography, video, material installations, and sculptural forms, the exhibition examines how bodily gestures, material imprints, and encounters with space function as sites of transformation. Drawing from personal memory, ritual, and ecological relationships, the work invites viewers into a contemplative environment where presence and absence coexist, and where material processes become pathways for reclaiming agency and belonging.

Parul Bhatia’s MFA thesis exhibition at SP/N Gallery has been supported in part by Center for Asian Studies at The University of Texas at Dallas.

title: Organic Worlds: Symbiogenesis in Art
description:
Organic Worlds: Symbiogenesis in Art

Feb. 7- April 28, 2026

SP/N Gallery

University of Texas at Dallas

https://bass.utdallas.edu/spn-gallery/

 

            Biology is more than genes, pharmaceuticals, and natural selection. Before any of these, biology is historical, modeled by where, when, and how it is written, bearing the legible marks of a cultural moment like rings on a tree or plaque on a tooth. Every quality of biology is thus situated in time and circumstance. Genes function properly inside of cells; drugs are profit engines for pharmaceutical companies; and natural selection is one circle of selective activity among others operating within earth’s atmosphere. So, life is almost always coupled to other life. It is symbiotic. Symbiogenesis is the leading theory of evolution, which is based on symbiotic cooperation between microbes occurring millions of years ago, as mitochondria and chloroplasts, organelles essential to the metabolism of animal and plant cells, bear the DNA of once free-ranging microbes.

Organic Worlds: Symbiogenesis in Art is an exhibition of art about biology understood from the perspective of context, collaboration, and coupling. It focuses on biological symbiosis in the artwork of Amy Youngs and Ken Rinaldo, setting in relief the significant role non-scientists play in writing biology. Exhibition artworks include two-dimensional works and time-based media that involve sound, touch, smell, immersion, amplification, and magnification.

Ken Rinaldo is internationally recognized for interactive AI bio-robotic art installations. He creates hybrid ecologies that integrate humans, machines, plants, animals, and more-than-human others, exploring idealized social and biological symbioses. Amy M. Youngs creates eco art, interactive sculptures, and digital media works that explore entanglements between technology, plants, and animals. Her interdisciplinary research involves empathy, relationships with non-humans, ecosystem construction, and seeing through the eyes of machines.

 

--Charissa N. Terranova, Curator of Organic Worlds: Symbiogenesis in Art and Margaret M. McDermott Distinguished Chair in Art and Aesthetic Studies at the Harry W. Bass Jr. School of Arts, Humanities, and Technology, University of Texas at Dallas

Organic Worlds: Symbiogenesis in Art is an exhibition of art about biology understood from the perspective of context, collaboration, and coupling. It focuses on biological symbiosis in the artwork of Amy Youngs and Ken Rinaldo, setting in relief the significant role non-scientists play in writing biology. Exhibition artworks include two-dimensional works and time-based media that involve sound, touch, smell, immersion, amplification, and magnification.

Ken Rinaldo is internationally recognized for interactive AI bio-robotic art installations. He creates hybrid ecologies that integrate humans, machines, plants, animals, and more-than-human others, exploring idealized social and biological symbioses. Amy M. Youngs creates eco art, interactive sculptures, and digital media works that explore entanglements between technology, plants, and animals. Her interdisciplinary research involves empathy, relationships with non-humans, ecosystem construction, and seeing through the eyes of machines.

 

--Charissa N. Terranova, Curator of Organic Worlds: Symbiogenesis in Art and Margaret M. McDermott Distinguished Chair in Art and Aesthetic Studies at the Harry W. Bass Jr. School of Arts, Humanities, and Technology, University of Texas at Dallas

title: Anxiety Toolbox Workshop #4
description:
A three-session workshop designed for people struggling with a variety of anxiety-related concerns. Sessions cover: 

  • Understanding what anxiety is and how it impacts us,

  • Exploring how thoughts and behaviors affect anxiety, and 

  • Developing strategies to better cope with anxiety.

 

To join, simply click the Comet Calendar link at the start time. If you’d like reminders and an easier check-in, you can also message us at sccgroups@utdallas.edu to be added to the roster.

Our workshops provide education and practical tools for managing common mental health concerns, similar to a training or class. Even though they are led by one of our therapists, workshops are not the same as therapy groups, as they are focused on learning and practicing skills rather than in-depth therapeutic process. All workshops are open to UTD students, and no group screening is required.

title: Collegiate Recovery Week's Dimension Days: Health
description:
Join the Center for Students in Recovery, the Student Counseling Center, the Student Wellness Center, the Basic Needs Resource Center, and the Student Health Center as we take part in recognizing Collegiate Recovery Week by exploring one of the four dimensions of recovery - health. SAMHSA (Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration) defines health in recovery as way to empower indivduals in making informed, healthy choices that support physical and emotional well-being.

During this event students will have the chance to create their own wellness kits! Departments will have items available such as condoms, menstrual products, toolbox cards, Temoc band-aids, tissues, small toiletry items and more! There will also be the opportunity for students to participate in puzzling and coloring.

The event will take place on Tuesday, April 14th from 1:00pm – 3:00pm at the first floor of the Student Union (by the pool tables).
No registration required. For any questions, please contact recovery@utdallas.edu.

We hope to see you there!

title: Understanding Self & Others - Process Group
description:
Understanding Self & Others is a weekly interpersonal process group for students who want to explore personal growth and increase self-awareness to enhance their experiences in personal and academic settings. In this safe space, group members can practice communicating more honestly and effectively with others while gaining support from peers. Group topics may include adjustment, loneliness, academic/general stress, and relationships.
 

Process groups are focused on the exploration and open processing and discussion of participants. Process groups are led by one of our therapists and typically more open-ended and less structured around a specific lesson or topic for the day. Clients are required to complete a group screening to assess whether the group matches their needs and interest.

For process groups, if you are not a current or recent client, please make an appointment to get started and note your interest in group therapy. You’ll complete intake paperwork and have a 30-minute “IC” (individual consultation) with one of our therapists, and then get scheduled for a brief screening meeting with the group’s leader.

If you are a current or recent client, reach out to our Groups & Workshops Coordinator at sccgroups@utdallas.edu to schedule a screening meeting.

title: The Music of Memory: Reconstructing a Lost Repertoire
description:
Register for a virtual talk on the occasion of Yom HaShoah. The virtual lecture will be presented by Francesco Lotoro, an internationally renowned pianist, composer, and musicologist dedicated to recovering music composed in ghettos, concentration camps, and other sites of captivity during World War II.

Since 1988, Mr. Lotoro has led a global effort to locate, reconstruct, and perform these lost works, preserving a powerful yet often overlooked dimension of Holocaust history. He is the founder of the Fondazione Istituto di Letteratura Musicale Concentrazionaria in Barletta and the author of the multi-volume KZ Musik- a comprehensive 24-CD encyclopedia set. 

Mr. Lotoro's talk explores how music created under extreme conditions functioned not as entertainment, but as a profound expression of inner life, resilience, and survival. Drawing on decades of archival research and performance, Lotoro reflects on the cultural and historical significance of this “concentrationary music” and its importance for understanding memory, identity, and artistic resistance in the twentieth century.
